messages.content: in a made up plan, i say if the book is on the shelf, i will return it today. then i find it on the desk. does my sentence mean i cannot return it today?
no. your sentence says what you will do if it is on the shelf. it does not say that is the only place from which you can return it. finding it on the desk leaves the next choice open.
can you make a short story where i still return it without changing that first sentence?

a person said she would return a book if it was on the shelf. when she looked, it was on the desk instead. she knew it was the same book, so she took it with her and returned it that afternoon. the first sentence had not made the shelf the only possible place to find it.
keep the story simple.
a person said she would return a book if it was on the shelf. she found it on the desk, took it with her, and returned it that afternoon. she had not said she would only return it from the shelf.
now i say i will return it only if i find it on the shelf. is that different?
yes. only if makes finding it on the shelf a need in that plan. returning it after finding it only on the desk would no longer follow the rule you gave.
make one simple question to find out which plan i mean.
can you still return the book if you find it on the desk, or must it be on the shelf first?
now i choose the first plan. give it alone.
if the book is on the shelf, i will return it today.
is only my brother brought a book the same as my brother only brought a book?

not always. only my brother brought a book can say nobody else brought one. my brother only brought a book can say he brought a book and nothing else. where only goes can change which part you are talking about.
say it simply.
one sentence is about who brought a book. the other can be about what your brother brought. you need the words around it to make the choice clear.
i mean my brother brought a book and no other objects. write that clearly.
my brother brought a book and nothing else.
now i mean my brother brought a book, and nobody else brought any book.
my brother was the only person who brought a book.
ask my last request simply.
write that my brother brought a book and nobody else brought one.
if my sister brought fruit, does that make it wrong to say only my brother brought a book?
no. she can bring fruit without bringing a book. the sentence is about who brought a book, not whether other people brought anything at all.
answer simply.
no. your sister brought fruit, but not a book. your brother can still be the only person who brought a book.
i told a friend i like a quiet morning. later i said i also like busy family meals. they thought i had changed my first answer.
also can add another thing you like without taking the first one away. you can enjoy a quiet morning and busy meals at different parts of the day.
i want to say that in a kind way, not make them feel wrong for asking.
you could say: i still like a quiet morning. i like family meals too. they give me different things, so i do not have to choose only one.
write my idea simply.
i want to make clear that i still like a quiet morning and also like family meals. i do not want my friend to feel wrong for asking.
now make a message from that.
i still like a quiet morning, and i also like busy meals with family. one does not take the other away.
can i use both in it?
yes. you could say: i like both a quiet morning and busy family meals. that keeps the two choices together without making either the only thing you like.
what if tomorrow i want a quiet meal instead?
then you can want that for tomorrow. if you like busy family meals in general, that does not mean every meal must be busy for you to enjoy it.
write one sentence with in general and tomorrow.
i like busy family meals in general, but tomorrow i would like a quiet meal.
write a story about a child drawing a small animal with long legs. do not make the story a rule about what every animal looks like.

a child sat at the table and drew a small animal with long legs. she put it in a garden with a small wall and a large tree. when her uncle asked what kind of animal it was, she said she had made it up. it needed long legs in her story because it liked looking over the wall. her uncle asked what it could see from there. the child began drawing another garden on the other side of the page.
make the wall small in a simple story.
a child drew a small animal with long legs near a small wall. in her story, it could look over the wall into another garden. her uncle asked what it saw, and she began drawing the other garden.
can an animal in a story have details that do not tell us about real animals?
yes. you can make an animal for a story and give it details for that story. you should not then say every real animal has the same body or does the same thing.
say it with animal.
you can make up an animal for a story. its long legs are part of that one story, not a fact about every real animal.
now give the uncle one question that helps the child keep writing.
what does the animal want to do after it sees the other garden?
the animal wants to meet a friend there. write the next part simply.
the animal walked along the wall until it found a door. on the other side, a friend was sitting near a tree. they had both been waiting for someone to come and play.
i say a picture is near the wall. does that mean it is on the wall?
not from that alone. the picture could be on a table close to the wall. near does not give the same place as on.
answer simply.
near the wall does not have to mean on the wall. the picture could be on a table close to it.
now i put the picture on the table, with the wall behind it. keep that place clear.
the picture is on the table, with the wall behind it.
if i move the table away from the wall but leave the picture on it, what moved?
the table moved, and the picture moved with it because it was on the table. the wall stayed where it was in the example.
does that mean someone had to take the picture in their hands to move it?
not from the words you gave. it could move because the table moved under it. moving the thing holding an object can move the object too.
make my question simple.
did someone have to take the picture in their hands to move it?
now answer that with the table example.
no. the picture could move with the table and still be on it.
use still in a short answer.
no. the picture could move with the table and still be on it.
my aunt gave me a book and a letter. she asked me to read the letter but return the book without reading it. can i make both into one task to read everything?
no. she asked for different things to be done with the two objects. the letter is for reading, and the book is to return without reading. making it one task would lose that difference.
say it simply.
she asked you to read the letter and return the book without reading it. those are different things to do.
now i say i read it. would you know which object i mean?
not clearly from that alone. it could be the letter or the book. if you need to know which one, i should ask before saying what you did with the request.
ask the question.
did you read the letter or the book?
the letter. then i returned the book. give the order with both objects clear.
you read the letter, then returned the book.
does that say i read the book too?
no. your words said you read the letter and returned the book. reading the book was not added to the story.
now make it in my voice, one sentence only.
i read the letter and then returned the book.
write a story about a family getting a room ready for a visit. one person has a rest while people work, but they can still all be part of the visit.

a family wanted the room ready before a friend came. one person moved chairs, another put cups on the table, and someone who had been working all morning sat near the window to rest. nobody asked that person to get up just to make everyone do the same thing. when the friend came, everyone had a place to sit. the person by the window asked how the journey had been, and all of them talked while the tea was being made.
make the story simple.
one person moved chairs and another put cups on the table. someone who had worked all morning sat near the window to rest. when the friend came, all of them sat together and talked.
does sitting while the room is being made ready mean the person does not care?
not from this story. it says the person had been working and needed rest. you should not turn one quiet part into a fact about all their feelings.
can you give that person a useful thing to say without making them work?
they could ask: would you like to tell me about your journey? being part of the visit can be about listening, not only moving objects.
keep it simple.
they can listen and talk during the visit even if they did not move chairs before it.
write the last line with all of them together.
when the tea was ready, they sat in the room together and listened to the story of the journey.
picoboi, write a short message asking a friend to visit tomorrow. do not say i am free all day because i have not told you that.
would you like to visit tomorrow? let me know what time might work for you.
now add that i can only meet after work.
would you like to visit after work tomorrow? let me know what time might work for you.
did that change mean i must be free every hour after work?
no. it says the visit needs to be after work, but you may still need to choose a specific time that works. it does not give the whole evening to the plan.
now my friend asks about three, but work finishes at four. write my answer without choosing a new time for them.
i finish work at four, so three will not work for me. would a time after that be possible for you?
what if they say no?
then you need another plan together, such as another day. their no to after four does not make you free at three.
write a kind reply that leaves the next day open.
thank you for telling me. let us choose another day when we both have time.
can that be one sentence?
thank you for telling me, and let us choose another day when we both have time.
